David Gareja

Sixth-century cave monasteries carved into a semi-desert ridge — the most unusual landscape in Georgia.

Time needed
3 h
From Tbilisi
75 km · 1:50
Road
Mostly paved
Car needed
Crossover / SUV
Season
All year
Entry
free

David Gareja lies south-east of Tbilisi on the Gareja ridge and looks nothing like the rest of Kakheti. Instead of vineyards and forest there is semi-desert: treeless, rolling, green for a few weeks in spring and a bleached yellow-grey for the rest of the year. The complex was founded in the sixth century by David Garejeli, one of the Assyrian Fathers, and grew over the centuries into dozens of separate monastic units scattered along the ridge.

The main and most accessible is the Lavra — a working monastery of terraced courtyards, cells cut into the rock face, a bell tower and David's tomb. From the Lavra a path climbs to the crest of the ridge and drops down the far side to the Udabno complex, where cave walls keep frescoes of the eleventh to thirteenth centuries. The round trip up and back takes roughly an hour and a half over steep, loose ground.

The landscape here is the attraction in its own right. From the crest an apparently endless steppe opens out, covered in flowers in April and May; tortoises, snakes and birds of prey are common sights. Spring is by far the best season — mild and green. A summer midday is hard going: there is effectively no shade and temperatures reach the high thirties.

Practical advice

Part of the complex runs along a disputed section of the border, and the climb up to the Udabno caves is periodically closed. This is routine rather than dramatic — ask at the Lavra gate when you arrive and you will be told the current situation; the Lavra itself is almost always open. Bring water, a hat and sun protection, since there is no shade anywhere on the ridge, and dress modestly for the monastery. The nearest café, ATM and toilet are back in Udabno village.

How to get there from Tbilisi

Leave Tbilisi either via Rustavi or via Sagarejo, then follow signs towards the village of Udabno — about 75 km and one hour fifty in total. Most of the route is paved, but the final stretch is rough and develops potholes after winter. In dry weather an economy car will get through; a crossover with higher ground clearance is far more comfortable and genuinely advisable after rain. The last dependable fuel is in Sagarejo — the following fifty kilometres are close to empty, so fill the tank before you turn off.
